results.title: Runpod vs Vast.ai vs Lambda: Which GPU Cloud Is Cheapest? · Aliteq
highlights:
Vast.ai, almost every time. On Nov 3, 2026 one H100 cost from $1.79 an hour on Vast.ai, $2.89 on Runpod and $3.29 on Lambda. Here is every card's price side by side, the extra charges each one adds, and when paying more is the smarter buy.

...

Which GPU cloud is cheapest for AI? Vast.ai, on almost every card. On November 3, 2026 the cheapest H100 on Vast.ai was $1.79 an hour, against $2.89 for an H100 PCIe on Runpod Secure Cloud and $3.29 for one H100 PCIe on Lambda. For an RTX 4090 it was $0.37 on Vast.ai and $0.89 on Runpod; Lambda doesn't rent 4090s at all. The lower price comes with a catch: Vast.ai is a marketplace of independent hosts, so reliability and extra fees vary by offer. Runpod costs more for a managed data center and an easier start. Lambda is built for multi-GPU training; it beats Runpod Secure Cloud on the B200 ($6.99 for one GPU, $6.69 per GPU on an 8x instance, against $7.99) but costs more for an H100.

## The short answer (read Nov 3, 2026)

Vast.ai is the cheapest of the three for almost every GPU. Read on November 3, 2026, an H100 started at $1.79 an hour on Vast.ai (median offer $2.33), $2.89 for an H100 PCIe on Runpod Secure Cloud, and $3.29 for a single H100 PCIe on Lambda. An RTX 4090 started at $0.37 on Vast.ai and $0.89 on Runpod Secure Cloud; Lambda has no 4090 or 5090. Runpod's older Community Cloud is cheaper ($0.34 for a 4090, $1.99 for an H100 PCIe), but Runpod no longer accepts new Community hosts. Lambda wins on the B200: $6.99 for one GPU and $6.69 per GPU on an 8x instance, against $7.99 on Runpod Secure Cloud.

- Watch the extras: Vast.ai bills storage while an instance is stopped and charges bandwidth per host

results.title: GPU Cloud Pricing Comparison 2026: H100, A100, RTX 4090 — AtmosCompute
highlights:
The dynamic nature of GPU cloud pricing is highlighted in the current rates for the H100, A100, and RTX 4090 GPUs. On-demand pricing reflects the flexibility of instant scaling without long-term commitments, with the H100 priced between $1.89 to $5.50 per hour. The A100, known for its balanced performance, ranges from $1.20 to $2.40 per hour. For more cost-effective needs, the RTX 4090 is priced at $0.30 to $0.80 per hour, making it an attractive option for various workloads. 

Spot instance pricing provides significant discounts, allowing users to capitalize on unused compute capacity. While this offers substantial cost savings, especially for non-critical workloads, there is also a risk of interruption. Reserved contract pricing, on the other hand, offers predictable costs and stability for long-term projects, appealing to businesses requiring consistent performance.

results.title: JPMorgan Report: AI Token and H100 GPU Prices Fall, Cost Pressure Eases | KuCoin
highlights:
JPMorgan’s July 2026 daily market report shows that AI token and H100 GPU prices have declined, easing cost pressures. Input token costs have decreased, while H100 utilization remains above 70%. Open-source models are gaining momentum, with increasing token usage and spending. H100 GPU rental prices dipped after seven consecutive months of increases, though they remain higher than those for A100s. HBM memory continues to be a bottleneck. The Fear & Greed Index suggests market sentiment is stabilizing amid these developments.

...

A similar structural differentiation has emerged in the GPU rental market.

In July 2026, the average rental price for H100 GPUs in the non-hyperscale cloud market was $2.68 per GPU hour, a 1.1% month-over-month decline. This marked the first monthly decrease after seven consecutive months of increases in H100 rental rates.

This decline is far below the 15% to 25% range and cannot be described as "H100 rental rates dropping by 20%." The report tracks the average monthly rental price per GPU hour, not the weekly rental price per card.

This indicates that the supply side is beginning to respond. More GPUs are entering the cloud rental market, intensifying competition among cloud service providers and computing power platforms, and short-term rental prices are no longer solely determined by extreme shortages. Compared to the phase of severe scarcity of high-end GPUs, the pressure of being unable to buy or rent, or having to wait in line for cards, has eased.

However, high-end resources remain expensive. The H100 is still significantly more expensive than the A100, and overall GPU utilization remains at 75%-90%, with high-performance GPU utilization exceeding 80%. As long as utilization stays within this range, the decline in rental prices appears more like the elimination of a portion of the scarcity premium rather than evidence of a broad oversupply of computing power.

...

For hardware and cloud service providers, the decline in short-term H100 rental rates signals a normalization of the exceptionally high returns driven by extreme shortages. Actual prices received by different customers can vary significantly due to long-term contracts, regional differences, bulk volume, and variations in spot price reporting methodologies. A mere look at the weekly average rental rate cannot directly imply that all cloud providers’ revenues will decline in tandem.

results.title: "H100 절반 값에 쓴다"…유휴 GPU 재임대 시장이 뜬다 - 디지털데일리
highlights:
[디지털데일리 박재현기자] 유휴 GPU(그래픽처리장치) 재임대 시장이 확대되고 있다. AI 서비스 수익화가 늦어지면서 인프라 고정비 부담을 안은 기업이 늘어난 영향이다. 몬드리안에이아이의 '런유어 AI', 베슬에이아이(VESSL AI)의 '베슬 클라우드'가 대표적이다.

두 서비스는 자체 GPU를 파는 방식이 아니다. 기업이나 기관에서 보유했지만 사용하지 않는 유휴 GPU를 수요자에게 판매할 수 있도록 중개하는 방식이다. 런유어 AI는 GPU 소유자와 수요자를 연결하는 중개형 플랫폼이다. 온디맨드와 장기계약을 함께 제공하며, 역경매 방식의 '리서브 클라우드'로 중소 데이터센터의 유휴 자원을 수익화한다. 베슬에이아이는 자체 데이터센터 없이 6개국 GPU를 연결하는 구조를 택했다. 현재 5000장 규모를 운용 중이며 연내 1만장까지 확대한다는 계획이다.

가격은 하이퍼스케일러보다 낮다. 런유어 AI는 H100 SXM 80GB를 시간당 3615원(3615C), B200을 9351원으로 책정했다. 베슬에이아이는 H100 온디맨드 요금이 시간당 2.98달러(약 4330원)로 하이퍼스케일러 절반 수준이라고 밝혔다.

대학 연구실과 스타트업이 주요 고객이다. 국내 한 대학 연구실 관계자는 "상용 퍼블릭 클라우드는 예산 한계가 명확했다"며 "재임대 플랫폼으로 같은 비용에 훨씬 큰 GPU 자원을 장기 확보했다"고 말했다.

수요 성격도 달라지는 추세다. 단기·소규모 대여보다 장기·대규모 대여 비중이 커지고 있다. 비용 절감보다 연구 확대를 위한 수요가 늘어난 결과다. 유휴 자원을 등록하는 공급 기업도 서서히 증가하고 있다.

자원 분할 방식에도 변화가 있다. GPU 한 대를 MIG(Multi-Instance GPU)로 쪼개 여러 사용자가 나눠 쓰는 방식은 줄었다. 여러 대를 묶어 성능을 확보하려는 수요가 늘면서 서버를 통째로 빌리는 베어메탈 방식 이용이 많아졌다.

시장 확대와 별개로 계약 리스크는 남아 있다. CSP 이용약관은 서비스 재판매와 전대를 금지한다. 네이버클라우드는 회사 동의 없이 제3자에게 서비스를 재판매·재임대할 수 없다고 규정했다. KT클라우드와 AWS도 동일한 취지의 조항을 두고 있다.

정식 플랫폼은 이 조항에 저촉되지 않는다는 입장이다. 홍대의 몬드리안에이아이 대표는 "자사는 CSP 임차 장비를 재임대하지 않는다"며 "CSP가 직접 공급하거나 기업이 자체 보유한 GPU를 재임대하는 형태"라고 말했다.

CSP 임차 장비를 재임대할 경우 최종 고객이 실제 사용하기 전까지 공급비를 받지 못해 수익 구조가 성립하지 않는다는 설명이다. 몬드리안에이아이는 최근 원소유주 확인과 실제 보관 장소 검증 절차를 강화했다.

results.title: The GPU Market Has Two Prices | GPUaaS.com
highlights:
A hyperscaler quotes $10.60 an hour for an H200. A wholesale buyer gets the same chip for $3.79 to $4.54. Neither number is fake. Both are real prices for the same GPU, quoted to two different buyers in two different markets.

...

- H100 retail held steady at $25,000 to $40,000 from mid-2024 into early 2026, while the secondary market swung from $50,000 during 2024's scarcity peak down to $21,000-$34,000 refurbished as of Q2 2026
- Hyperscaler H200 on-demand runs around $10.60/hr versus $3.79 to $4.54/hr wholesale for the same silicon
- A100 cloud rental rates range $1.29 to $3.43/hr depending on provider, nearly a 3x spread for the same chip
- The retail price is quoted to whoever asks casually. The clearing price moves with real-time supply and demand among buyers actually transacting
- Q2 2026 secondary supply is loosening further as B200 deployments accelerate, with continued softening expected on H100 and A100 inventory specifically

...

The same split shows up in rental rates, not just purchase price. Hyperscaler on-demand carries a premium built for buyers who need the full managed stack, global region coverage, compliance certification, native tooling. Specialized providers price the same H200 silicon closer to what the hardware costs to run, without the bundle. Both numbers are legitimate. They're pricing different things wrapped around the same chip.

...

The A100 tells the same story from a different angle. Cloud rental rates for A100 now range $1.29 to $3.43 an hour depending on provider, a spread wide enough that the cheapest and most expensive quotes for the same chip differ by nearly 3x. Purchase prices for used A100s are projected to fall another 10 to 15% through the rest of 2026 as more enterprises move to Blackwell-generation hardware. Every generation this happens to. The retail number for the current chip stays put while the secondary and rental markets for it, and for whatever it's replacing, move constantly underneath.

...

For H200, hyperscaler on-demand runs around $10.60 an hour versus $3.79 to $4.54 an hour wholesale for the same silicon. For A100 rentals, rates range $1.29 to $3.43 an hour depending on provider, nearly a 3x spread. These gaps vary by chip generation and current market conditions.

results.title: Blackwell GPU rental prices hit $4.08 an hour. Sixty days earlier, they were 48% cheaper. | Jonathan Mather
highlights: Blackwell GPU rental prices hit $4.08 an hour. Sixty days earlier, they were 48% cheaper. Not over a year. Over two months. AWS's flagship 8x H200 instance went from $34.61 an hour to $39.80 in the same stretch. Lead times for data-center GPUs now run 36 to 52 weeks. Order today, plan for delivery next year, if it clears at all. A training run budgeted at $40,000 on reserved capacity is now $80,000 to $120,000 on-demand, if the capacity is reachable at any price. Here's why it's scarce, and it doesn't resolve itself. Microsoft, Google, Meta, and Amazon placed multi-billion-dollar forward orders for Blackwell chips that already consumed most of Nvidia's available allocation through 2027. That's not four companies competing for GPUs alongside you. That's four companies who bought the shelf before you got to the store. This isn't a future risk. The compute shortage is already causing outages at Anthropic and has forced OpenAI to cancel products. If the two best-capitalized AI companies on the planet are getting squeezed this hard, paying a premium to route around it isn't a real option for anyone smaller. Memory prices are surging at the same time. TSMC capacity is effectively sold out. Power infrastructure is now a hard bottleneck in its own right. Every layer of the stack tightened at once. Bank of America's own projection: demand outstrips supply through 2029. Not a temporary crunch. A multi-year structural gap. If your AI roadmap assumes 2025 pricing and 2025 availability, it's already obsolete. The real question isn't "can we afford the GPU-hours." It's whether your architecture depends on owning or reserving compute at all, because the companies with the deepest pockets just found out the answer is no, not reliably. Has the compute shortage already hit your roadmap, or are you still budgeting off last quarter's numbers?

results.title: Cheapest Cloud GPU in 2026: Every Card at Live Prices | FastGPU
highlights:
As of November 14, 2026, the cheapest NVIDIA H100 SXM you can rent on demand is $1.84 per GPU-hour at Vast.ai. The cheapest hyperscaler rate for the identical card is $5.38 at Google Cloud, which is 2.9x the floor ($5.38 / $1.84), and the dearest on-demand listing for it is $12.29, 6.7x the floor. Further down the range the pattern repeats: a 24 GB RTX 4090 rents from $0.14 at Vast.ai, while its dearest listing is $0.99 ( 7.1x). The same chip, for the same hour, is on sale across that whole range at once, and where you land in it decides most cloud GPU bills.

...

An hourly rate is a unit price. What a job costs is that unit price times the units the provider bills, plus everything it bills beside the GPU. Most "cheapest GPU" comparisons stop at the unit price, which is how a team ends up paying more for a job on the card with the lowest rate. The gap between the two numbers comes from six places: how the meter ticks, the smallest machine you can rent, what the rate includes, data and storage, whether the card is in stock and whether the job survives an interruption. The first five are covered here and interruption has its own section after this one.

...

Providers bill GPU time in different increments: per second, per minute or per hour, and many add a minimum charge per start ( billing increment). On a per-second meter a 7-minute job costs 7 minutes. On an hourly meter it costs an hour. The table lists the meters of providers whose own documentation states them, as we read it on October 29, 2026; renting GPUs by the minute and by the second cover every tracked provider.

...

Spot (also called preemptible or interruptible) is the same GPU sold for less on the condition that the provider can take it back when it needs the capacity, usually with a short warning ( spot). Against a provider's own on-demand rate, the discount is the figure providers advertise, and the live figures say how large it is. On the H100 SXM right now, AWS's spot rate is -88% against its on-demand rate, Google Cloud's -80%, CoreWeave's -60% and Verda's -50%. The spot vs on-demand page lists every provider's spot discount, card by card.

But the comparison that matters to a buyer is spot against the whole market's on-demand floor, not against the same provider's on-demand rate, and there spot is not automatically the cheaper line. A marketplace host renting a card on demand can undercut a big cloud's spot capacity, because the host's price is set by competition among hosts rather than as a discount on a cloud's list price. On-demand is the right default for anything that runs less than most of the day. For a steady load that runs around the clock for months, reserved capacity trades a commitment for a lower hourly rate ( reserved capacity), and the arithmetic of whether it pays is one division. A reservation is owed every hour whether the GPU works or not, so it beats on-demand only if the GPU would otherwise be busy for more than the reserved rate divided by the on-demand rate of all hours. Hyperstack's reserved H100 SXM rate is $2.72 against its own on-demand rate of $3.20 ( -15%), so the break-even share is 0.85 ($2.72 / $3.20): reserving pays only if the GPU would be busy for more than that share of all hours, and never if the share is 1 or more.

There is no single cheapest cloud GPU, only the cheapest one for a given memory size, job shape and moment. As of November 14, 2026, the market lists the same H100 SXM from $1.84 to $12.29 per GPU-hour and the same RTX 4090 from $0.14 to $0.99, and those ranges, not the cards, are where the money is. The cheapest hour is usually found by sizing the job to the smallest memory tier that holds it, reading every live offer in that tier, and only then looking at the rate.

The cheapest job takes one more step: the hourly rate times what the provider actually bills, plus what it bills ... Spot is a discount on a provider's own rate, not always on the market's, and a reservation is a price for certainty, not a guarantee of the lowest rate.

results.title: JPMorgan Analysis: Token and H100 Prices Drop Together, Is AI Cost Cooling Down? | WEEX Crypto News
highlights:
A report from JPMorgan's " Data Center Watch" released in July shows that the prices for AI inference calls and high-end GPU short-term rentals cooled down simultaneously at that time.

...

## H100 Rental Prices Decline, But High-End Cards Are Not in Oversupply

The GPU leasing market has also seen similar structural differentiation.

In July 2026, the average rental price of H100 in the non-hyperscale cloud vendor market was $2.68 per GPU hour, a month-on-month decrease of 1.1%. This marks the first month-on-month decline after seven consecutive months of rising H100 rental prices.

This drop is far less than 15% to 25% and cannot be described as "H100 rental prices have dropped by 20%". The report tracks the average monthly rental price calculated per GPU hour, not the weekly rental price per card.

This indicates that the supply side is beginning to respond. More GPUs are entering the cloud leasing market, intensifying competition among cloud service providers and computing power platforms, and short-term rental prices are no longer solely determined by extreme shortages. Compared to the phase of high-end GPU scarcity, the pressure of not being able to buy, rent, or queue for cards has eased somewhat.

However, high-end resources are still not cheap. H100 prices remain significantly higher than A100, and overall GPU utilization remains at 75%-90%, with high-performance GPU utilization exceeding 80%. As long as utilization remains in this range, the decline in rental prices seems more like the elimination of some scarcity premiums rather than an indication that computing power supply is fully in excess.
